In the Monday review at the design studio, Pradeep put up his hand before anyone spoke. "The measurements on slide six are mine and they're wrong. Nobody asked, but I couldn't let it go out." He looked tired, not embarrassed. Swati felt her ears burn. Last week she had spotted the same error in her own file and fixed it at midnight, telling no one, because her first thought had been how the team would talk. Their manager said, "Thank you, though next time tell me before the meeting."
At the tea machine Swati said, "You didn't seem to care what people would think." Pradeep laughed. "I cared. I just cared more about sleeping tonight." She thought of the colleagues who might have copied her old figure.

qa.q: On which slide were Pradeep's measurements wrong?
qa.a: The measurements on slide six were wrong.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when Pradeep admitted the error?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, because she had quietly fixed the same kind of error and told nobody.

qa.q: What could Swati try that keeps her care for the team's view but adds what Pradeep showed?
qa.a: She could tell the team or the manager about her own catch, so others can check their figures, while still thinking about how it is said.

qa.q: What does the manager's remark suggest about Pradeep's way of speaking up?
qa.a: The manager thanked Pradeep but asked to be told beforehand, which suggests that speaking up openly without warning has a cost even when honest.

grounding: A person raised with shame norms sees another person at the studio driven by conscience, and each approach shows strengths and blind spots.

Dear Pankaj,

You asked how the new job is. Odd and interesting. Two colleagues have taught me something without meaning to. Leila will not submit a report until she is sure nobody could find fault. I recognise that; it comes from me too. Tomas, on the other hand, told our manager about his own slip when no one would ever have known, and went home lighter.
I grew up counting who was watching. Tomas seems to count what he can live with. Neither is perfect: Leila's polish sometimes keeps the whole team waiting, and Tomas can confess before he has checked whether the fix is ready. I am trying to borrow a little from each, to think of the people around me and of my own conscience too.
Write soon.

Swati

qa.q: Which colleague told the manager about a slip when no one would have known?
qa.a: Tomas told the manager about a slip when no one would ever have known.

qa.q: What does Swati feel when recognising Leila's habit?
qa.a: Swati feels a mixed, rueful kinship, because the wish to avoid any fault, watched by others, comes from Swati too.

qa.q: What is Swati trying to do after seeing both colleagues?
qa.a: Swati is trying to borrow a little from each: keep thinking of the people around and also listen to conscience, to avoid the weakness each shows.

qa.q: What are the drawbacks of Leila's approach, as seen by the team?
qa.a: Leila's polish sometimes keeps the whole team waiting, because the report is not submitted until nobody could find fault.

grounding: A person raised with shame norms observes colleagues who fear their own conscience, and sees strengths and blind spots in each.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage:
Ujjwal, you asked what it's like working with my Dutch team. The funniest thing I've noticed is how differently we feel bad about mistakes.
When Maarten missed a deadline, he said, "I let the team down. I feel bad about it," even though no one was angry. It was his own conscience talking. Nobody needed to know for him to feel it.
When I missed one, my first thought was: what will my manager think? What will people say at the coffee machine? I'm Dilnaz, and I was raised on "what will people say."
I've been watching this for a year. Their way means they own mistakes quickly. But sometimes they don't notice when they've hurt someone's feelings in public. Our way makes us careful with each other's dignity, but sometimes we hide mistakes to save face.
I think I'm learning to take the best of both. Own it inside. Protect people's face outside.

qa.q: What did Maarten say when he missed a deadline?
qa.a: He said, "I let the team down. I feel bad about it."

qa.q: What does Dilnaz feel when she makes a mistake at work?
qa.a: Dilnaz first feels anxious about what the manager and colleagues will think, rather than an inner sense of guilt.

qa.q: What does Dilnaz decide to take from each culture?
qa.a: Dilnaz aims to own mistakes inside, like her Dutch colleagues, and protect people's dignity outside, as she learned at home.

qa.q: How might Maarten see Dilnaz's worry about what people say?
qa.a: Maarten might find it puzzling, since for him guilt comes from his own conscience, not from others' opinions.

grounding: A young adult raised with shame norms observes guilt-oriented colleagues and sees the strengths and blind spots of each.

I've worked beside Rekha for two years at the call centre in Gurugram, and I've watched her change how she talks about mistakes.
Our new team lead, Sachin, came from our Canada office. When someone made an error, he'd say, "Own it, fix it, move on," and he meant it. Rekha told me once over lunch, "At home, when I made a mistake, my mother would say, 'What will the neighbours think?' Here, nobody talks about neighbours. It's all about what I think of myself."
I noticed she started admitting errors faster in meetings. But I also noticed that Sachin sometimes corrected people loudly in front of everyone, and Rekha winced for them. Once she said to me, "He means well. But in our culture, you don't take someone's face in public."
I don't know exactly what she felt. But she started taking Sachin aside, quietly, to suggest private feedback. He listened.

qa.q: Where did Sachin come from?
qa.a: Sachin came from their Canada office.

qa.q: What might Rekha have been feeling when she winced?
qa.a: Rekha probably felt uncomfortable and sympathetic, seeing colleagues embarrassed by being corrected loudly in public.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that combined the strengths of both cultures?
qa.a: She began owning her own mistakes quickly, like Sachin, while suggesting he give feedback privately to protect people's dignity.

qa.q: How might Sachin see Rekha's suggestion?
qa.a: Sachin may be surprised at first but open, since he listened and may not have realised that public correction hurt people.

grounding: A colleague observes a young adult raised with shame norms noticing both her own culture's and a guilt-oriented manager's strengths and blind spots.

passage:
Monday. At the German firm's Pune office, Ojas, twenty-four, watched his manager announce, "I made an error in the budget. My fault. I'll fix it by Friday." No one blinked. Ojas was amazed. His father, Jagdish, had never admitted a mistake in front of anyone.
Wednesday. At home, his father had forgotten to pay the society bill. When a neighbour mentioned it, Jagdish said, "The bank must have made a mistake." Later, he quietly paid it and told Ojas, "Never let people see you slip."
Friday. Ojas thought about both. The manager's honesty made fixing things fast. His father's care for face made the neighbours trust him and kept arguments polite. But hiding slips could make them bigger.
That evening, he told his father about the manager. Jagdish was quiet, then said, "Maybe I could have just said I forgot." Ojas smiled.

qa.q: What did the manager say about the budget?
qa.a: He said, "I made an error in the budget. My fault. I'll fix it by Friday."

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when no one blinked at the manager's admission?
qa.a: Ojas felt amazed and curious, because his father had never admitted a mistake in front of anyone.

qa.q: What did Ojas notice about the strengths and blind spots of each approach?
qa.a: Owning mistakes openly made fixing things fast, while caring about face kept relationships polite, but hiding slips could make them bigger.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel when he says "Maybe I could have just said I forgot"?
qa.a: Jagdish seems thoughtful and a little softened, open to seeing another way.

grounding: Over one week, a young adult observes his manager's guilt-oriented honesty and his father's face-saving, and sees strengths and blind spots in both.

passage: Devika, you're nervous about joining the Berlin team? Let me tell you what I learnt there at your age. In my first month I made an error in a shipping report. I panicked about what the team would think, who might have seen, whether my manager would mention it in the meeting. My colleague Jonas made a similar error the same week. Nobody had noticed his. He walked into the manager's office anyway and said, "I got this wrong. I couldn't sleep." I was amazed. At home in Pune we were raised on "what will people say". He was raised on "what will I say to myself". But that same month Jonas missed his mother's birthday for a deadline, and nobody in his family said a word. I found that lonely. Each way has a gift and a gap, beta. Your Madhuri Aunty learnt to keep both.

qa.q: What did Jonas say to the manager?
qa.a: He said, "I got this wrong. I couldn't sleep."

qa.q: What was young Madhuri feeling after her error in the shipping report?
qa.a: She panicked, anxious about what the team would think and who might have seen.

qa.q: Which choice in the story shows the strength of the conscience-driven way?
qa.a: Jonas owning up to an error nobody had noticed shows conscience working without an audience, which builds honesty.

qa.q: How did Jonas seem to experience his own mistake?
qa.a: Jonas seemed troubled by his own conscience rather than by others' eyes; he lost sleep even though nobody had noticed.

grounding: It illustrates someone raised with shame norms who, working beside a colleague guided by conscience, sees that each way has strengths and blind spots.
